name: Toyotomi Hideyoshi
info: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, born a peasant's son in Owari Province in 1537 according to tradition, rose in Oda Nobunaga's service, completed the unification of Japan by 1591, became regent, and launched the invasions of Korea in 1592.

facts.born: According to tradition, 17 March 1537 (the 6th day of the 2nd month of Tenbun 6) in Nakamura, Owari Province, now Nakamura Ward in Nagoya; son of Kinoshita Yaemon, an ashigaru, with no traceable samurai lineage
facts.died: 18 September 1598 at Fushimi Castle; his death was kept secret by the Council of Five Elders to preserve morale
facts.role: Retainer of Oda Nobunaga; daimyo from 1573; kampaku (Imperial Regent) from 1585, the first commoner to hold the post; daijo-daijin (Chancellor of the Realm) from 1586; taiko (retired regent) from 1592 until his death
facts.known: avenging Oda Nobunaga at the Battle of Yamazaki in 1582; completing the unification of Japan by 1591; Osaka Castle; the sword hunt of 1588; the land surveys and the class system; the Bateren Edict against Christian missionaries; the invasions of Korea from 1592; the tea ceremony and the Golden Tea Room

t: Born with no surname to a peasant who served as a foot soldier, Hideyoshi rose through Oda Nobunaga's service and, after Nobunaga's death in 1582, became the first commoner to hold the post of kampaku.
He subdued Shikoku, Kyushu and the Kanto and finished the unification of Japan in 1591, disarmed the peasantry, and ordered land surveys and a census that formed the basis of systematic taxation.
His invasions of Korea from 1592 ended in stalemate and exhaustion, and after his death in 1598 his young son Hideyori was displaced by Tokugawa Ieyasu, who founded the Tokugawa shogunate.
dyk: Hideyoshi never took the title of shogun. He arranged to be adopted by Konoe Sakihisa, one of the highest-ranking members of the Fujiwara clan, and in 1586 the Imperial Court gave him the new clan name Toyotomi.
ev: Hideyoshi is born in Nakamura, Owari Province, according to tradition, the son of an ashigaru
He becomes an ashigaru of the Oda clan, then headed by Oda Nobunaga, and soon Nobunaga's sandal-bearer
Nobunaga appoints him daimyo of three districts in northern Omi Province, where he builds Nagahama Castle
Nobunaga dies in the Honno-ji incident; Hideyoshi defeats the assassin Akechi Mitsuhide at the Battle of Yamazaki
He becomes kampaku and conquers Shikoku; Osaka Castle's main enclosure is finished
The Siege of Odawara against the Later Hojo; the following year the Kunohe rebellion completes the unification
He takes the title of taiko and launches the invasion of Korea
Hideyoshi dies at Fushimi Castle; the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 displaces his son Hideyori

sections.early:
According to tradition, Hideyoshi was born on 17 March 1537 (the 6th day of the 2nd month of Tenbun 6) in Nakamura, Owari Province, now Nakamura Ward in Nagoya, during the Sengoku period, as the Ashikaga shogunate collapsed. He had no traceable samurai lineage. His father, Kinoshita Yaemon, was an ashigaru, a peasant employed by samurai as a foot soldier, and Hideyoshi had no surname. His childhood given name was Hiyoshimaru, though variations exist. Yaemon died in 1543, when Hideyoshi was seven years old.

Contemporary writings by Ankokuji Ekei and by Kakukane Ue, a retainer of the Shimazu clan, confirm his poor background, and Ekei noted that he had begged in the streets. Many legends describe his being sent to study at a temple as a young man; he rejected temple life and went in search of adventure. Under the name Kinoshita Tokichiro he first joined the Imagawa clan as a servant to a local ruler named Matsushita Yukitsuna. In 1558 he became an ashigaru for the Oda clan, the rulers of his home province of Owari, then headed by the ambitious Oda Nobunaga. He soon became Nobunaga's sandal-bearer, a position of relatively high status. His biographers say he also managed the kitchen and supervised repairs to Kiyosu Castle, though the latter claim has been called "apocryphal".
sections.rise:
In 1561 Hideyoshi married Nene, the adopted daughter of Asano Nagakatsu. In 1564 he found success as a negotiator, persuading several Mino warlords to desert the Saito clan, largely through bribery, among them the clan's strategist Takenaka Shigeharu. Nobunaga's easy victory at the Siege of Inabayama Castle in 1567 was largely due to his efforts, and in 1568 he became one of Nobunaga's most distinguished generals and took the name Hashiba Hideyoshi. At the Battle of Anegawa in 1570 he was assigned to lead Oda troops into open battle for the first time. In 1573 Nobunaga appointed him daimyo of three districts in northern Omi Province; he built Nagahama Castle and took control of the gunsmithing village of Kunitomo, whose output of firearms increased dramatically under his administration. Later Nobunaga sent him to conquer the Chugoku region from the Mori clan.

On 21 June 1582, during the Siege of Takamatsu, Nobunaga and his eldest son Nobutada were killed in the Honno-ji incident. Hideyoshi made peace with the Mori and, eleven days after Nobunaga's death, defeated the assassin Akechi Mitsuhide at the Battle of Yamazaki on 2 July 1582, taking Nobunaga's authority and power for himself. He chose Nobunaga's infant grandson Oda Hidenobu as heir, and in 1583 destroyed the forces of Shibata Katsuie at the Battle of Shizugatake, after which he controlled some 30 provinces. The same year he began Osaka Castle on the site of the temple Ishiyama Hongan-ji. In 1584 the Battle of Komaki and Nagakute against Tokugawa Ieyasu and Oda Nobukatsu ended in a stalemate, although Hideyoshi's forces suffered heavy losses.
sections.deeds:
Like Nobunaga before him, Hideyoshi never achieved the title of shogun. He arranged to be adopted by Konoe Sakihisa and secured the post of Imperial Regent (kampaku) in 1585 and Chancellor (daijo-daijin) in 1586, when the Imperial Court gave him the clan name Toyotomi. He built the Jurakudai palace in 1587 and entertained the reigning Emperor Go-Yozei the following year. After the earthquake of 1586 forced him to abandon a campaign against Ieyasu, he sent his sister and his mother to Ieyasu as hostages, and Ieyasu travelled to Osaka and expressed his intention to submit. His forces took Shikoku from Chosokabe Motochika in 1585 and Kyushu from the Shimazu clan in 1587, with 200,000 soldiers against the Shimazu's 30,000. He won the Siege of Odawara in 1590 and, in 1591, crushed the Kunohe rebellion, which completed the unification of Japan.

In 1588 he forbade peasants to own weapons and launched a sword hunt; the confiscated weapons were melted down into building material for the Hall of the Great Buddha at the Hoko temple in Kyoto. The measure effectively stopped peasant revolts and ensured greater stability at the expense of the freedom of the individual daimyo. He ordered comprehensive land surveys and a census, required samurai to live in castle towns, and in 1590 banned slavery, though contract and indentured labour persisted. He lavished time and money on the tea ceremony and had a portable Golden Tea Room made.
sections.opponents:
Hideyoshi's rise and rule met resistance, and some of his measures were violent. In 1585 his forces attacked Negoro-ji, set the complex aflame and cut down monks as they escaped the burning buildings. An uprising in the Yokote Basin in 1590 opposed the land survey conducted by his government; it was suppressed and proved disastrous for the Onodera clan. At the Kunohe rebellion in 1591 the rebel leader Kunohe Masazane surrendered and was executed with the castle defenders. After Komaki and Nagakute, Ieyasu's general Sakakibara Yasumasa circulated a manifesto condemning Hideyoshi's conduct as a betrayal of Nobunaga's wishes and insulting his origins, and Hideyoshi offered 100,000 kan for the general's head. In 1591 he ordered the tea master Sen no Rikyu to commit suicide, possibly in a fit of anger.

In 1587 he issued the Bateren Edict ordering the expulsion of Christian missionaries. The edict is described as a response to several perceived threats, among them Catholic forces that, according to the historian Paul E. Eckel, had sacked Buddhist temples in Kyushu, and the trafficking of people; according to the historian Arata Harumasa, at least 50,000 Japanese were sold overseas as slaves around that time, mainly by Portuguese merchants. In late 1596 he had twenty-six Christians arrested; they were tortured, mutilated and paraded through towns, and on 5 February they were crucified in Nagasaki.

His nephew Hidetsugu, whom he had adopted and made kampaku, was in August 1595 stripped of his titles, exiled to Mount Koya and ordered to commit suicide, which he did on 20 August. Hideyoshi then had members of Hidetsugu's family, including 31 women and several children, beheaded in Kyoto.
sections.last:
Hideyoshi's only son, three-year-old Tsurumatsu, died in September 1591, after his half-brother Hidenaga had died of illness in February. He adopted his nephew Hidetsugu in January 1592 and resigned as kampaku to take the title of taiko. Adopting Nobunaga's dream of a Japanese conquest of China, he began an invasion of Korea in 1592, intending to conquer Korea and eventually Ming China. Seoul fell to Konishi Yukinaga on 19 June, and within four months his forces had reached the border of Manchuria. A Ming army sent in 1593 recaptured Pyongyang, and the Japanese navy was destroyed by Admiral Yi Sun-sin, which ended Japan's ability to resupply its troops in Seoul. In 1593 Hideyoshi's second son Hideyori was born.

Konishi Yukinaga and the Ming envoy Shen Weijing forged Hideyoshi's memorial to the Ming court, on which basis the Ming agreed to invest him as King of Japan. When the deception came to light in 1596, he was enraged, and in 1597 he ordered a renewed invasion, which met with less success; Japanese troops remained pinned down in Gyeongsang Province. All three parties to the war were exhausted. Hideyoshi told his commander in Korea, "Don't let my soldiers become spirits in a foreign land."

He died at Fushimi Castle on 18 September 1598. His last words to his closest daimyo and generals were "I depend upon you for everything. I have no other thoughts to leave behind. It is sad to part from you." The Council of Five Elders kept his death secret and ordered the forces in Korea to return to Japan.
sections.legacy:
After Hideyoshi's death the Council of Five Elders was unable to keep Tokugawa Ieyasu's ambitions in check. Kato Kiyomasa and Fukushima Masanori, who had served in Korea, returned to find Ishida Mitsunari in power, held in contempt by them, and sided with Ieyasu. Hideyori lost the power his father had held, and Ieyasu's Eastern Army defeated Mitsunari's Western Army at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600. Appointed shogun in 1603, Ieyasu attacked Osaka Castle in 1614 and 1615, forcing Hideyori and his mother Yodo-dono to commit suicide, which ended the Toyotomi clan. Historians generally attribute the weakening of the regime mainly to the loss of all his adult heirs, which left only the five-year-old Hideyori.

Hideyoshi changed Japanese society through a rigid class structure, restrictions on travel and surveys of land and production; the land surveys formed the basis for systematic taxation. Ieyasu left in place the majority of his decrees and built his shogunate upon them. Hideyoshi also influenced material culture. During the Korean campaigns large quantities of prized ceramic ware were confiscated and many Korean artisans were forcibly relocated to Japan. Politically he set up a system that balanced the most powerful daimyo, with a council of the most influential lords and a regent in command.

Osaka Castle, the sword hunt and the temples he built and restored in Kyoto remained. By 1915 he had been posthumously raised to Senior First Rank. In a letter to his wife he wrote that he was ready for a long siege and wished to return in triumph and leave a great name behind him.

summary: Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537–1598), a peasant's son, rose through Oda Nobunaga's service, avenged him in 1582 and completed the unification of Japan by 1591. He disarmed the peasantry and surveyed the land, then invaded Korea in 1592; after his death Tokugawa Ieyasu displaced his heir.
notes: Birth: the article says 'according to tradition' 17 March 1537 (given as Julian); start 1537 with circa true.
Names are written without macrons in the file where they appeared in plain ASCII form; check the 'Kato Kiyomasa' line in legacy for a stray character and normalise to the site's usual spelling.

Left out: the film, television, anime and game sections; the family lists beyond Tsurumatsu, Hidetsugu and Hideyori; the Tenshō-Jingo war; Hideyoshi's Noh performances; the failed Taiwan tribute attempt (the article's wording is brief and unclear); the Tokugawa Jikki account of his deathbed regret, which is a later record.
Nene's birth years are given as 1541/1549 and the second son Hideyori's mother as Yodo-dono; not used.
The article gives Hideyoshi's age-of-heir wording as 'five-year-old Hideyori' in 1598 while Hideyori was born in 1593; consistent.

The edict's purposes are listed in the article as alternatives ('to exert greater control over the Kirishitan daimyo or to prohibit human trafficking'); both are given as perceived threats and not chosen between.
Ban on slavery 1590 and the sale of 50,000 Japanese overseas are both in the article; the article does not link them, and none is claimed.
